scenes.text: Our survey's in. Twelve students charge their phones in their bedrooms, and eight charge them somewhere else, and the bedroom group reported less sleep. Then this headline turns up. Phones in bedrooms steal two hours of sleep! It sounds like exactly what we found. It isn't. Even a fair sample can be let down by how the data were collected, and by what people claim afterwards. So what can go wrong when we collect data?

Look at how our data were collected. We didn't tell anyone where to charge their phone. We just asked. That's an observational study, just watching what happens. Observational studies are useful, but they have a big weakness. The two groups can differ in other ways too. Remember the early bus? In our sample, five of the six bus students charge their phones in their bedrooms. Bus students get up earlier. So the bedroom group might sleep less because of the bus, not the phone. Something else could explain the difference. That's why an observational study can show that two things happen together, but it can't show that one causes the other.

To test whether the phone itself makes a difference, you'd run a controlled experiment. That means you change one thing on purpose, and keep everything else the same. Take forty volunteers. A random draw puts twenty of them in a group whose phones charge in the kitchen for two weeks, and the other twenty carry on as usual. The random draw is the key. It spreads the bus students, and everything else, across both groups, three bus students in each. If the kitchen group then sleeps more, the phone is the likely reason. Experiments have faults too. If people choose their own group, all six bus students might end up together. People might sneak their phones back, or sleep differently because they know they're being watched. And two weeks might be too short, or forty volunteers might not represent Year 11.

Now the practical side. Picture the whole process as a pipeline, from the question, to the people, to the method, to the recording, to the claim. Faults can creep in at every stage. The question might be unclear, like our old overlapping buttons. Some people chosen for the sample might not reply. If five of our twenty don't answer, and they're the ones who slept least, the results look better than they are. People guess and round. Ask about sleep, and lots of answers come back as whole hours. Someone might type seven point five as seventy-five, and suddenly a student slept seventy-five hours. And timing matters. A survey in exam week, or after a long weekend, describes that week, not a normal one. The fix is to plan for each stage, follow up the people who didn't reply, and check the data before you use it.

The last stage is the claim, and this is where the headline goes wrong. A misrepresentation presents results so they seem to show more than they do. Steal says the phone causes it, but ours was an observational study. Phones in bedrooms suggests every teenager, but we asked twenty students at one school, on one night. Our survey found a smaller difference, and only on average. Percentages can mislead too. Sixty per cent of students sleep with their phone sounds huge, but it's twelve out of twenty. Misunderstandings happen on the other side, when people read a result, or a question, differently from what was meant. Hours slept might be read as hours in bed. Here's an honest version. In our sample of twenty Year 11 students, those who charged their phones in their bedrooms tended to report less sleep. That doesn't show the phone caused it.

So whenever you judge a data collection, walk the pipeline. Is the question clear? Did the right people answer, and did enough of them reply? Was it an experiment or an observational study, and does the claim match? Were the answers recorded and checked? And does the claim stay inside what the sample and method can show? Every yes makes the results easier to trust.

Here's the card. Check the question, the people, the method, the recording and the claim. And remember, an experiment changes one thing on purpose, while an observational study just watches. Only a fair experiment can show cause.

Your turn. A school finds that students who eat breakfast at the school canteen get higher marks, and claims that canteen breakfasts raise marks. Is this an experiment, or an observational study? Then give one reason the claim may be wrong. Pause here to answer.

Nobody was told to eat breakfast there. The school just recorded what happened, so it's an observational study. The claim may be wrong because something else could explain both. Students who arrive early for breakfast might be more organised, or get more sleep. Calling it an experiment because marks were measured is the slip.
Last one. A phone company texts ten thousand customers at two in the morning. Rate our network from one to ten. Two hundred reply. Describe two faults in this data collection. Pause here to answer.

First, non-response. Only two hundred of ten thousand replied, two per cent, and they chose to, so the very happy or very annoyed are over-represented. Second, timing. A text at two in the morning misses or wakes most customers, so night owls answer most. Saying two hundred replies is plenty is the slip.

Our data are collected, and checked. Each student's answers now sit in a record sheet. Hours of sleep. How many screens are in the bedroom. Where the phone charges. How rested they feel. And how they get to school. Some answers are numbers, and some are words. Which ones can we average, and which can we only count? That's next.
